notes: Ruling slot 1 = Unificación Nacional (Trejos). Coalition template slot 2 holds the PLN (opposition, Figueres) following MD placement; the real coalition partners are Ulate's PUN (16) and Calderón's PRN (14). Vanguardia Popular (4) is banned; its legal front PASO sits in 18.

0.name: Los Amigos de Somoza
0.text:
Los Amigos de Somoza is the network of Costa Rican exiles, ranchers and former partisans who looked to the Somoza family in Managua after losing the 1948 civil war. Many joined the failed January 1955 invasion launched from Nicaraguan soil, and they still keep ties across the northern border in Guanacaste. On 1 January 1970 they hold no office and operate as an informal circle on the fringe of the governing coalition.

They want a strong hand against communism and organised labour, close security cooperation with Washington and Managua, and an end to what they call the weakness of the unarmed republic. Their leverage lies in cattle money, cross-border contacts and Nicaraguan patronage.

1.name: Partido Unificación Nacional
1.text:
The National Unification Party is the alliance of Otilio Ulate's National Union Party and the calderonista republicans that carried José Joaquín Trejos Fernández to the presidency in 1966. On 1 January 1970 it governs, but Trejos cannot seek re-election and the coalition has nominated former president Mario Echandi Jiménez for the February election against José Figueres.

Unificación stands for fiscal restraint, private enterprise, Catholic social values and firm alignment with the United States and the Central American Common Market. It draws on coffee growers, merchants, the Catholic middle class and the rural calderonista vote, and its leverage rests on the presidency and a solid bloc in the Legislative Assembly.

2.name: Partido Liberación Nacional
2.text:
The National Liberation Party is Costa Rica's largest party, founded in 1951 by José Figueres Ferrer, victor of the 1948 civil war and abolisher of the army. In opposition since 1966, it enters 1970 as the clear favourite, with Figueres seeking a second presidency and Daniel Oduber Quirós as its leading parliamentarian.

Liberación champions the interventionist social state built since 1949: nationalised banking, autonomous public institutions, electrification and expanding social security. Firmly anti-communist and close to the Democratic Left of the Americas and the Alliance for Progress, it is nonetheless open to trade with the Soviet bloc to find buyers for coffee. Its strength lies in the public sector, teachers, smallholders and an unrivalled party machine.

3.name: Confederación Costarricense de Trabajadores Rerum Novarum
3.english: Rerum Novarum Confederation of Costa Rican Workers
3.native_full: Confederación Costarricense de Trabajadores Rerum Novarum
3.text:
The Rerum Novarum Confederation of Costa Rican Workers was founded in 1943 by the priest Benjamín Núñez to give Catholic workers an alternative to the communist-led unions. After 1948 it became the labour arm of the victors, and Núñez himself rose within the National Liberation Party. On 1 January 1970 it is one of the main legal confederations, rooted among urban and public-sector workers.

It follows Catholic social teaching and social-democratic trade unionism: collective bargaining, the labour code, minimum wages and social security. It works with the inter-American free trade union network against communist influence on the banana plantations, and its leverage lies in its ties to Liberación deputies.

4.name: Partido Vanguardia Popular
4.text:
The Popular Vanguard Party is the communist party of Costa Rica, led since the 1930s by Manuel Mora Valverde. Allied with Calderón Guardia in the 1940s and defeated in the 1948 civil war, it is outlawed under Article 98 of the 1949 Constitution. On 1 January 1970 it remains banned and contests the February election through the legal Socialist Action Party.

Vanguardia follows the Soviet line of peaceful coexistence and a gradual, electoral road. It demands land reform, nationalisation of the banana and mining concessions, and diplomatic relations with Moscow. Its base lies among banana workers on both coasts, the Limón docks and a layer of urban intellectuals.

5.name: Federación de Estudiantes de la Universidad de Costa Rica
5.english: Federation of Students of the University of Costa Rica
5.native_full: Federación de Estudiantes de la Universidad de Costa Rica
5.text:
The Federation of Students of the University of Costa Rica is the elected voice of students at the country's only university in San Pedro de Montes de Oca. On 1 January 1970 it is radicalising fast, as a new generation inspired by Cuba, Vietnam and the 1968 student revolts turns against the two-party establishment.

Its activists denounce foreign investment, the banana companies and the bauxite concession under negotiation with ALCOA, and call for an anti-imperialist alliance of students and workers. Ideologically it mixes New Left, Guevarist and Trotskyist ideas. Its leverage lies in its capacity to fill the streets of San José and to shape the next political generation.

6.name: Bloque de la Victoria
6.text:
Bloque de la Victoria was the 1943 electoral pact between Rafael Ángel Calderón Guardia's republicans and the communists of Manuel Mora, sealed with the blessing of Archbishop Víctor Sanabria. Defeated in 1948, its memory survives in 1970 among old calderonista unionists and veterans who never accepted the order of Figueres.

They regard the social guarantees and labour code of the 1940s as a revolution stolen by Liberación and Washington. They favour state-led welfare, a pact with organised labour, trade with the socialist countries and distance from the United States. Their leverage lies in loyal working-class neighbourhoods of San José and in sentimental ties to Calderón himself.

7.name: Los Mariachis
7.text:
Los Mariachis are the veterans of the irregular forces that fought for the government of Teodoro Picado and Calderón Guardia in the 1948 civil war. Disarmed and scattered after the defeat, they persist on 1 January 1970 as a resentful network in the countryside and the poorer quarters of the capital.

They despise the Second Republic of Figueres as the creation of foreign-backed liberators and dream of a caudillo who would settle accounts with Liberación. With no use for parliamentary niceties, they favour authoritarian order and a break with the American tutelage of the 1948 settlement. Their leverage lies in hidden weapons, personal loyalties and street muscle.

8.name: Los Comerciantes de Tiro
8.text:
Los Comerciantes de Tiro is a small circle of Lebanese Shia traders from the Tyre region who settled in San José and Puntarenas alongside the larger Christian Lebanese community. On 1 January 1970 they gather in private homes for prayer and Ashura commemorations and follow news of Musa al-Sadr's new Supreme Islamic Shia Council in Beirut.

They favour a modern, reformist Shia identity built on education, mutual aid and the dignity of the Lebanese south, while remaining law-abiding residents who keep out of Costa Rican partisan quarrels. Their influence rests on commercial networks, remittances and family ties stretching to Lebanon and West Africa.

9.name: Los Lectores de Nayaf
9.text:
Los Lectores de Nayaf is a tiny group of young Lebanese Shia immigrants in San José who pass around pamphlets and recorded sermons from the seminaries of Najaf. On 1 January 1970 they are known to almost nobody outside their own families and meet quietly in the back rooms of shops.

They are drawn to the teaching of the exiled Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini on Islamic government, which calls for jurists to rule in place of kings. They reject both American and Soviet models and see the Shah of Iran and Israel as enemies. Their leverage is negligible beyond devotion and links to clerical networks abroad.

10.name: Los Amigos del Rey Faisal
10.text:
Los Amigos del Rey Faisal is a small circle of Arab Muslim merchants and visiting preachers in San José who look to Saudi Arabia and the Muslim World League for guidance and funds. On 1 January 1970 it has no mosque, only a prayer room and occasional literature sent from Mecca.

It teaches quietist, establishment Sunni Islam: obedience to lawful rulers, strict personal piety and avoidance of political agitation. It is firmly anti-communist and sympathetic to King Faisal's pan-Islamic diplomacy. Its leverage lies in modest Saudi donations, business respectability and good relations with the authorities.

11.name: Los Estudiantes del Califato
11.text:
Los Estudiantes del Califato is a handful of Palestinian and Jordanian students and young traders in San José who have come into contact with Hizb ut-Tahrir, the Liberation Party founded in Jerusalem by Taqiuddin al-Nabhani. On 1 January 1970 they meet as a private study circle with no public presence.

They regard every existing state as illegitimate and call for the restoration of a single caliphate for all Muslims. Hostile to Israel, the United States and Soviet atheism alike, they reject elections and party politics. Their only assets are conviction and contact with the party's cells in the Middle East and Europe.

12.name: Los Hermanos de Palestina
12.text:
Los Hermanos de Palestina is a circle of a few devout Muslim families of Palestinian and Syrian origin in Costa Rica who sympathise with the Muslim Brotherhood of Hasan al-Banna. On 1 January 1970 it organises Quran lessons, charity for the refugees of the 1967 war and readings of Sayyid Qutb.

It calls for the moral renewal of society through preaching, education and charity, and hopes for Islamic government achieved by gradual, lawful means. It opposes Zionism, Western materialism and communist atheism. Its leverage lies in welfare networks and solidarity collections for Palestine among the wider Arab community.

13.name: Las Autónomas
13.text:
Las Autónomas is the power bloc of the autonomous institutions created after 1948: the Costa Rican Electricity Institute, the National Production Council, the Social Security Fund, the housing institute and the nationalised banks. On 1 January 1970 their managers and engineers form a technocracy that outlasts every change of government.

They believe in planning, public enterprise and expert administration insulated from party politics, and they distrust both the communists and the free-market purists. Neutral in foreign affairs, they seek loans and know-how wherever they find them. Their leverage lies in budgets, jobs and control of electricity, credit and social insurance across the country.

14.name: Partido Republicano Nacional
14.text:
The National Republican Party is the party of Rafael Ángel Calderón Guardia, president from 1940 to 1944 and author of the social guarantees, the labour code and the University of Costa Rica. Defeated in 1948, Calderón returned from exile, and in 1970 his republicans form one pillar of the governing National Unification coalition.

Calderonismo combines Catholic social teaching with populist welfare and a deep hostility toward Figueres and Liberación. It defends social security, cheap credit for small farmers and the authority of the Church. Its base lies among rural voters, older workers and Catholic families personally loyal to Calderón, and its leverage rests on that inherited loyalty.

15.name: Cámara de Industrias de Costa Rica
15.english: Chamber of Industries of Costa Rica
15.native_full: Cámara de Industrias de Costa Rica
15.text:
The Chamber of Industries of Costa Rica represents the factory owners who have prospered behind the tariff walls of the Central American Common Market. Alongside it stand the coffee barons, sugar planters and import houses that have dominated the economy since the nineteenth century. On 1 January 1970 it is one of the most influential lobbies in San José.

It demands protection for local industry, cheap credit, limits on labour costs and a voice in the management of the nationalised banks. It is firmly pro-American and anti-communist. Its leverage lies in investment decisions, newspaper ownership and close ties to deputies of both main parties.

16.name: Partido Unión Nacional
16.text:
The National Union Party is the party of Otilio Ulate Blanco, president from 1949 to 1953 and owner of the Diario de Costa Rica. Its 1948 election victory, annulled by the Calderón-controlled Congress, triggered the civil war. On 1 January 1970 it is a partner in the governing National Unification coalition.

Ulatismo stands for classical liberalism: limited government, fiscal orthodoxy, private enterprise and suspicion of the growing autonomous institutions. It is resolutely pro-American and anti-communist. Its voters are urban professionals, merchants and conservative coffee growers, and its leverage lies in Ulate's prestige and his influence over the press.

17.name: Centro Científico Tropical
17.text:
The Tropical Science Center is a private scientific association founded in San José in 1962 by Leslie Holdridge, Joseph Tosi and fellow researchers to study and protect Costa Rica's tropical forests. On 1 January 1970 it runs ecological surveys, advises on land use and works alongside the national parks office created by the 1969 Forestry Law.

It warns that cattle ranching and logging are destroying the forests at alarming speed and calls for protected reserves, watershed management and scientific land planning. It is non-partisan and international in outlook. Its leverage lies in expertise, foreign research funding and growing respect among young officials.

18.name: Partido Acción Socialista
18.text:
The Socialist Action Party is a legal electoral front formed for the 1970 elections so that the outlawed Popular Vanguard and other socialists can stand candidates. On 1 January 1970 it campaigns for the February vote with Manuel Mora Valverde at the head of its list, gathering independent socialists, teachers and unionists who reject the Cold War blocs.

It calls for agrarian reform, nationalisation of foreign concessions, defence of the public institutions and an independent foreign policy including relations with the socialist countries. Its base is the banana zones, urban unions and the university. Its leverage lies in a disciplined militancy far larger than its vote.

19.name: Los Pekinistas
19.text:
Los Pekinistas are the small Maoist groups among students and young teachers in San José who broke with Popular Vanguard after the Sino-Soviet split. On 1 January 1970 they are fragmented into study groups and clandestine printing presses, active on campus and in a few rural unions.

They denounce Moscow's peaceful coexistence and Vanguardia's electoralism as revisionism, and preach a protracted people's war based on the peasantry. They are hostile to the United States and the Soviet Union alike and look to Beijing and Tirana. Their leverage is minimal outside the university, but their militancy attracts radical youth.

20.name: Los Echandistas
20.text:
Los Echandistas are the personal followers of Mario Echandi Jiménez, president from 1958 to 1962 and the National Unification candidate in the February 1970 election. Echandi built his reputation on plain speech, austerity and open defiance of Liberación's bureaucracy, and he remains the most popular figure of the anti-Figueres camp.

They speak for the small farmer and taxpayer against party machines and the swelling public payroll, mixing anti-communism with suspicion of the San José elites. They demand spending cuts, honest administration and order. Their leverage lies in Echandi's personal popularity in the provinces and his place at the head of the opposition ticket.

21.name: Movimiento Costa Rica Libre
21.text:
The Free Costa Rica Movement is a militant anti-communist organisation founded in 1961 in response to the Cuban Revolution. On 1 January 1970 it is legal and well financed, organising rallies, propaganda and paramilitary training groups and campaigning against any opening to the Soviet bloc.

It combines Catholic integralism, fierce nationalism and paramilitary discipline, and treats communists, student radicals and much of Liberación as a single subversive threat. Close to business circles and American anti-communist networks, it is ready to take to the streets. Its leverage lies in money, its shock groups and its influence over sections of the press and the security forces.

22.name: Guardia Civil
22.text:
The Civil Guard is the national police force that has taken the place of the army since José Figueres abolished the military in December 1948. Commanded by political appointees who change with each government, it numbers a few thousand men and on 1 January 1970 answers to the Trejos administration.

Officially it has no political role, and Costa Ricans are proud of their unarmed republic. Yet some officers trained at American schools in the Panama Canal Zone resent their low status and amateurism and argue for a more professional force against subversion. Its leverage lies in being the only armed body in the country.

23.name: Los Imperialistas de Cartago
23.text:
Los Imperialistas de Cartago take their name from the party that wanted Costa Rica to join Agustín de Iturbide's Mexican Empire and was defeated by the republicans of San José at Ochomogo in 1823. In 1970 the label survives as a nostalgic Hispanist circle of old Cartago families, Catholic scholars and admirers of Spain.

They cultivate the colonial heritage of the old capital, admire Franco's choice of Juan Carlos de Borbón as heir in 1969, and speak of order, faith and hierarchy above party strife. Their influence is limited to salons, lay brotherhoods and the columns of conservative newspapers.
